newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU suspends planned wheat export tax, no new date.
newsitem.headline: EU suspends planned wheat export tax, no new date.

text.p: The European Commission, due to French opposition, suspended plans on Wednesday to tax daily soft wheat grain and flour exports, leaving it uncertain whether the move will go ahead, a European Commission official said.

The tax had been aimed at saving scarce supplies for EU domestic consumers and dampening prices which had surged on concern over world crop prospects following frost in the United States and dry weather in Europe.

But EU sources said that French European Commissioner Edith Cresson objected, saying that the tax was no longer needed because world wheat prices have since fallen and there was no longer a danger of an exodus of European wheat abroad.
Unanimity among the 20 commissioners was required to adopt the proposal for taxes of 15 Ecus a tonne on exports of soft grain and 20 Ecus a tonne on wheat flour under a so-called written procedure.
"It's suspended, there's no new deadline," the Commission official said. "It can be reopened but it's not sure. We don't know what will happen now."
Exporters who have taken out a nil value export licence will be liable to tax if they have not customs-cleared their grain and flour exports before the tax is approved.

The official said the EU's cereals management committee, made up of delegates from member states, would discuss the question of an export tax at their next meeting on May 15, but a final decision was up to the Commission.
Meanwhile the Commission would continue to reject all requests for wheat export licences.
On April 24, the committee supported the move, which is aimed at saving supplies for domestic consumers and dampening prices which had risen some 20 percent above EU support levels.
However France, Germany and Austria voted against and three other countries abstained.
On April 17, the EU closed a weekly tender for this season's wheat exports, several weeks earlier than usual.

The EU started 1996/97 with a wheat export tax when stocks were low and prices high but restored export refunds in September when prospects of bumper crops in the main producer countries dampened world prices.
